claims.text: Reliable formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials is governed by in situ evolution of their atomic-scale structure and composition.
Catalytic performance is governed by in situ evolution of the nanomaterials' atomic-scale structure and composition.
In situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy can monitor and elucidate the evolution of atomic-scale structure and composition.
In situ transmission electron microscopy can monitor and elucidate the evolution of atomic-scale structure and composition.
Evolution of atomic-scale structure and composition during catalysis produces active sites.
The active-site-forming structural and compositional evolution optimizes catalytic performance.
Use of in situ characterization will result in a 20% increase in reaction rate relative to the material tested without in situ characterization.
Use of in situ characterization will result in a 15% improvement in product-yield selectivity relative to the material tested without in situ characterization.
The proposed relationship should hold from 250°C to 350°C.
The proposed relationship should hold from 0.5 atm to 1.5 atm.
The proposed relationship should hold at reactant flow rates from 5 to 15 mL/min.
The relationship between atomic-scale state and catalytic performance may depend on reaction conditions and material composition.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis presents in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy and electron microscopy as observational tools for monitoring the proposed mediator, but the controlled comparison treats their presence as the causal intervention expected to improve activity and selectivity. No mechanism explains why measurement itself should generate the proposed structural evolution or performance gains.

The rule equates 'not significantly different' with p-value < 0.05, whereas under the conventional significance criterion p < 0.05 denotes a statistically significant difference; failure to detect a significant difference would ordinarily be p >= 0.05.

Reliable material formation is attributed to evolution observed during catalysis, although the intervention occurs after the material is already described as synthesized. The experiment therefore does not directly test reliability of initial material formation.
